los.text: Describe the natural factors that limit clot formation (protein S, protein C, fibrinolysis) and the genetic and environmental factors that alter this process
los.html:
Natural anticoagulants
  • Antithrombin: inactivates thrombin (IIa) and Xa (and IXa, XIa); activity ↑ ~1000× by heparin.
  • Protein C (vitamin K-dependent): thrombin binds thrombomodulin on endothelium → activates protein C (with EPCR) → activated protein C + cofactor protein S cleave and inactivate factors Va and VIIIa.
  • Tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI): inhibits TF–VIIa and Xa.
  • Intact endothelium: NO, prostacyclin (PGI₂) (anti-platelet), heparan sulfate, ADPase.
Fibrinolysis
  • Endothelial tPA (and urokinase) converts plasminogen → plasmin (mainly on fibrin surface) → degrades fibrin → fibrin degradation products/D-dimer.
  • Regulated by PAI-1 and α2-antiplasmin, TAFI.
Inherited thrombophiliasFactor V Leiden (commonest in Caucasians, ~5%; factor V resistant to activated protein C), prothrombin G20210A (↑ prothrombin), deficiencies of protein C, protein S, antithrombin (rarer, more severe).
Acquired/environmental factors(Virchow's triad: stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability)
  • Surgery
  • Immobility
  • Long-haul travel
  • Malignancy
  • Pregnancy and puerperium
  • Combined oestrogen pill/HRT
  • Obesity
  • Smoking
  • Age
  • Dehydration
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome
  • Nephrotic syndrome (antithrombin loss)
  • IBD
  • Myeloproliferative disorders
  • PNH
  • HIT
  • COVID-19
  • Central lines.
Warfarin-induced skin necrosisEarly ↓ protein C (short half-life) before other factors → transient prothrombotic state (hence heparin bridging when starting warfarin for VTE).

los.text: Describe primary and secondary haemostasis and assess normal blood clotting
los.html:
Primary haemostasis (platelet plug, seconds–minutes)
  • Vascular injury
  • → vasoconstriction
  • → exposed subendothelial collagen
  • → platelet adhesion (GPIb binds von Willebrand factor on collagen; GPVI to collagen)
  • → activation (shape change, release of ADP, thromboxane A₂, serotonin)
  • → aggregation (GPIIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen bridging platelets).
Secondary haemostasis (coagulation cascade → fibrin)
  • Cell-based model: initiation (tissue factor + VIIa → small amounts of Xa → thrombin) → amplification (thrombin activates platelets, V, VIII, XI) → propagation (tenase VIIIa–IXa and prothrombinase Va–Xa on activated platelet surfaces → thrombin burst) → fibrinogen → fibrin, cross-linked by XIIIa.
  • Classical: extrinsic (TF, VII) → PT; intrinsic (XII, XI, IX, VIII) → APTT; common pathway (X, V, II, I).
  • Vitamin K-dependent: II, VII, IX, X (+ protein C, S). Ca²⁺ required.
Assessing clotting
TestMeasuresProlonged by
Platelet countNumberThrombocytopenia
PT / INRExtrinsic + common (VII)Warfarin, liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, DIC
APTTIntrinsic + common (VIII, IX, XI, XII)Heparin (UFH), haemophilia A/B, vWD (sometimes), lupus anticoagulant
FibrinogenClauss assay↓ in DIC, massive haemorrhage
Thrombin timeFibrinogen → fibrinHeparin, dabigatran, low fibrinogen
D-dimerFibrin breakdown↑ in VTE, DIC, infection, surgery, pregnancy (sensitive, not specific)
  • Also bleeding history (scores)
    • PFA-100
    • platelet function tests
    • vWF assays
    • mixing studies (factor deficiency corrects; inhibitor doesn't)
    • viscoelastic tests (TEG/ROTEM) in major haemorrhage.

los.text: Describe the most common causes, pathophysiology, investigations and principles of treatment of abnormal blood coagulation
los.html:
Bleeding disorders

Platelet type(mucocutaneous: petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, menorrhagia, gum bleeding)
  • ITP (autoimmune; isolated low platelets)
  • Drugs (aspirin, clopidogrel)
  • Marrow failure
  • Von Willebrand disease (commonest inherited bleeding disorder; AD; ↓ vWF → platelet adhesion defect and ↓ VIII).
Coagulation type(deep bleeds: haemarthroses, muscle haematomas, delayed bleeding)
  • Haemophilia A (VIII) and B (IX), X-linked recessive, ↑ APTT, normal PT
  • Liver disease
  • Vitamin K deficiency (malabsorption, newborn → vitamin K at birth)
  • Anticoagulants
  • DIC (sepsis, malignancy, obstetric: consumption → ↓ platelets, ↑ PT/APTT, ↓ fibrinogen, ↑ D-dimer).
Rx
  • Treat cause
  • Tranexamic acid
  • Desmopressin (mild haemophilia A/vWD type 1)
  • Factor concentrates (VIII, IX; emicizumab prophylaxis)
  • Platelet transfusion
  • FFP/cryoprecipitate (DIC)
  • Vitamin K
  • IVIg/steroids (ITP).

Thrombosis

Venous(DVT/PE)Stasis + hypercoagulability; red (fibrin, RBC-rich) thrombi. Arterial (MI, stroke): atherosclerotic plaque rupture + platelets; white thrombi.
Ix
  • Wells score → D-dimer if unlikely
  • Compression USS (DVT), CTPA (PE; V/Q if renal impairment/pregnancy).
  • Thrombophilia testing only selectively (unprovoked VTE with strong FHx, young, unusual sites).
Rx
  • Anticoagulate: DOAC (apixaban/rivaroxaban) first line
  • LMWH in pregnancy/cancer (or DOAC in cancer)
  • Duration 3 months if provoked, ≥6 months/long term if unprovoked.
  • Thrombolysis for massive PE with haemodynamic compromise.
  • Arterial: antiplatelets, revascularisation.
Antiphospholipid syndromeLupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2GP1 antibodies + arterial/venous thrombosis or pregnancy loss → warfarin (DOACs not recommended, especially triple positive).

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of drugs used to modulate haemostasis and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
sessions: Clin 4: Pharmacology of haemostasis and thrombosis
los.html:
DrugMechanismMonitoring / reversalNotes
AspirinIrreversible COX-1 inhibition → ↓ TXA₂ (platelet lifespan ~7–10 days)—GI bleeding; ACS, secondary prevention
Clopidogrel / prasugrel / ticagrelorP2Y12 (ADP receptor) antagonists—DAPT after ACS/stents; clopidogrel is a prodrug (CYP2C19)
GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors (tirofiban)Block fibrinogen binding—High-risk PCI
Unfractionated heparinPotentiates antithrombin (IIa and Xa)APTT; reverse with protamineIV, short half-life; HIT risk; renal failure, peri-procedure
LMWH (enoxaparin, dalteparin)Antithrombin → mainly XaAnti-Xa (if needed); partially reversed by protamineSC; VTE prophylaxis/treatment, pregnancy; renal dosing
FondaparinuxAntithrombin-mediated Xa inhibitionACS (NSTEMI)
WarfarinVitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1) inhibitor → ↓ II, VII, IX, XINR (target 2.5 VTE/AF; 3.5 recurrent/mechanical mitral); reverse with vitamin K + prothrombin complex concentrateMany interactions (CYP2C9), diet; teratogenic; mechanical valves, APS
DOACs: apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban (Xa inhibitors), dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor)Direct inhibitionNo routine monitoring; reversal: andexanet alfa (Xa), idarucizumab (dabigatran)Fixed dosing; renal adjustment; not for mechanical valves/APS
Thrombolytics (alteplase, tenecteplase)tPA → plasminogen to plasminSTEMI (if no PCI), ischaemic stroke (within 4.5 h), massive PE; bleeding risk
Tranexamic acidAntifibrinolytic (blocks plasminogen lysine binding sites)Trauma (CRASH-2), PPH, menorrhagia, surgery
  • Evidence: aspirin in secondary prevention (~25% relative ↓ events)
    • DOACs non-inferior to warfarin with less intracranial haemorrhage (AF trials)
    • AF anticoagulation via CHA₂DS₂-VASc vs bleeding risk (ORBIT/HAS-BLED).

los.text: Describe the general processes and factors influencing healing in tissues (include resolution, regeneration, and repair)
los.html:
Resolution
  • Complete restoration of normal tissue when injury is mild/short-lived and the architecture is intact (e.g. lobar pneumonia resolving).
  • Exudate removed by lymphatics, macrophages clear debris, mediators decay.
Regeneration
  • Replacement of lost cells with the same type of cells. Depends on cell type:
  • Labile (continuously dividing: epithelia of skin and gut, haematopoietic cells) → regenerate well.
  • Stable/quiescent (G0, can re-enter cycle: liver, kidney tubules, fibroblasts, smooth muscle) → regenerate if scaffold (basement membrane/reticulin) intact.
  • Permanent (non-dividing: neurons, cardiac myocytes) → can't regenerate → scar.
Repair (fibrosis/scarring)
  • Replacement by connective tissue when damage is extensive or cells can't regenerate.
  • Granulation tissue (new capillaries via angiogenesis (VEGF), fibroblasts, macrophages, oedema)
  • → collagen deposition (type III → type I)
  • → remodelling (MMPs)
  • → scar with ~70–80% of original tensile strength at best.
Skin wound healing
  • Haemostasis → inflammation (neutrophils → macrophages) → proliferation (granulation tissue, re-epithelialisation, myofibroblast contraction) → remodelling (months).
  • Primary intention (clean, opposed edges, sutured) vs secondary intention (gaping wound; more granulation tissue, contraction, larger scar).
Factors impairing healing
  • Local: infection, poor blood supply (ischaemia, PAD), foreign body, movement, haematoma, radiation, pressure.
  • Systemic: age, diabetes, malnutrition (protein, vitamin C for collagen hydroxylation, zinc), glucocorticoids, chemotherapy, smoking, obesity, anaemia.
Abnormal healingHypertrophic scar (within wound boundary), keloid (beyond boundary; Afro-Caribbean), contractures, wound dehiscence, chronic ulcers.
